A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {D, \sqsubseteq}$ be a [[Definition:Complete Partial Order|complete partial order]] with [[Definition:Bottom (Lattice Theory)|bottom]] $\bot$.
Let $F: D \to D$ be [[Definition:Scott-Continuous Mapping|Scott-continuous]].
Then $F$ has a [[Definition:Least Fixed Point|least fixed point]]:
:$\displaystyle \map {\operatorname {lfp} } F = \bigsqcup_{n \mathop \ge 0} \map {F^n} \bot$

B_source.statement:
Let $\struct {L, \preceq}$ be a [[Definition:Complete Lattice|complete lattice]] and $F: L \to L$ [[Definition:Increasing Mapping|increasing]].
Then:
:$\map {\operatorname {lfp} } F = \inf \set {x \in L: \map F x \preceq x}$
exists.

substitutions.least fixed point as inf of pre-fixed po: least fixed point as sup of the iterate chain

object_map.reformulation: Add the continuity hypothesis to Tarski's monotonicity, which upgrades the abstract existence to the concrete iterative construction.

validity_conditions: F monotone gives an increasing chain bottom <= F(bottom) <= F^2(bottom) <= ...; the cpo guarantees its sup exists.
Scott-continuity lets F commute with this sup, so the sup is a fixed point, and monotonicity makes it the least one.
This strengthens Tarski (which needs only monotonicity for existence) with continuity to get the formula - a specialization by added hypothesis.
proof_plan: By the [[Knaster-Tarski Theorem]], a least fixed point exists when $F$ is monotone on a complete lattice.
Assume in addition that $F$ is [[Definition:Scott-Continuous Mapping|Scott-continuous]], so $F$ preserves suprema of [[Definition:Chain (Set Theory)|chains]].

As $\bot \sqsubseteq \map F \bot$ and $F$ is monotone, by [[Principle of Mathematical Induction|induction]]:
:$\bot \sqsubseteq \map F \bot \sqsubseteq \map {F^2} \bot \sqsubseteq \cdots$
This chain has a supremum $x^* = \displaystyle \bigsqcup_n \map {F^n} \bot$ in $D$.

By continuity:
:$\displaystyle \map F {x^*} = \bigsqcup_n \map {F^{n + 1} } \bot = x^*$
If $\map F y = y$, then $\map {F^n} \bot \sqsubseteq y$ for all $n$ by induction, so $x^* \sqsubseteq y$.
Hence $x^* = \map {\operatorname {lfp} } F$, which is the [[Kleene Fixed-Point Theorem]].
{{qed}}
